title: A 7–2 hold as mortgage rates tighten and inflation undershoots the April forecast
summary: The June decision left Bank Rate at 3.75%. Seven members supported a hold. Megan Greene joined Huw Pill in voting for 4%. Their dissent came as headline inflation fell, and the committee marked down its near-term forecast. It reflected a judgement about the cost of embedded inflation and the durability of private borrowing-rate increases. A stronger preference for insurance can coexist with a weaker central inflation reading when the evidence about next year’s pay bargaining has barely begun to arrive (minutes, paragraphs 22–34).

Since April, Brent and UK wholesale gas had averaged $100 per barrel and 116 pence per therm. Following news of a possible Middle East agreement, they fell to about $79 and 100 pence respectively shortly before the meeting. Both remained above their pre-conflict comparisons. Crude oil also gave an incomplete picture of costs for UK users. Diesel and jet-fuel spreads over crude remained elevated, fertiliser and metals were dearer and some freight measures had risen. Strategic reserve releases, fuel substitution and deferred energy demand had softened the immediate impact. These buffers left uncertainty over the duration of the shock even after the risk of another abrupt spike eased (paragraphs 2–4 and 24).

May CPI inflation was 2.8%, the same as April and 0.4 percentage points below the April Report forecast. Food inflation of 2.2% was a substantial part of the downside news. Using prices at the close on 15 June, staff expected inflation a little below 3% in the third quarter and a little above 3¼% in the fourth. The next regulated household energy cap would rise 13.5% to £1,862. Firms’ expected own-price inflation a year ahead fell from 4.4% in April to 4.0% in May, still 0.6 percentage points above February. The Bank/Ipsos household one-year measure moved the other way over the longer interval, from 3.2% in February to 4.0% in May. Identical endpoints in two surveys refer to different respondents and different prices (paragraphs 8–12).

Labour costs supplied a reason to wait. Private regular average weekly earnings rose 2.9% in the three months to April from a year earlier. Agents expected basic private pay settlements to average 3.5% for 2026, with few existing deals likely to reopen. Firms’ year-ahead wage-growth expectation was steady at 3.4%. The economy grew 0.6% in the first quarter, but staff estimated underlying quarterly growth near 0.2%. Falling vacancies, near-flat underlying employment growth and signs of capacity underuse fit a gradually loosening labour market. That evidence mattered to the bargaining power of workers. It said less about the demands they might bring to a fresh round of pay talks after another winter of higher utility bills (paragraphs 13–17 and 25–27).

The clearest measured transmission was already in household and business financing. The UK two-year overnight-indexed swap rate stood about 70 basis points above pre-war levels, quoted two-year fixed mortgage rates about 80 points higher and investment-grade corporate yields about 50 points higher. The median survey respondent expected the policy rate to stay flat for the year ahead. Simply removing the rate cuts previously expected tightened that survey path by about 50 basis points. Shortly before the meeting the market curve still rose around 30 points towards the end of 2026. Staff models attributed much of that slope to risk premia. These are changes accumulated since the conflict, not returns caused by the June announcement (paragraphs 5–7 and 28–30).

Six hold voters saw evidence that disinflation had been proceeding before the war. The seventh, Mann, saw greater upside risks but believed policy could transmit quickly enough to wait. Greene worried that the cost of discovering next year that feedback was strong could exceed the cost of reversing a precautionary increase. Pill stressed catch-up behaviour as firms and workers defended margins and purchasing power. Both questioned whether market tightening would persist without a change in Bank Rate. A reversal in private funding costs, a change in wage expectations or evidence of weak sales could each shift a future vote for a different reason (paragraphs 31–35).

questions.question: How much of the higher mortgage quote reached the household budget by June?
questions.detail: Distinguish advertised rates for new fixed mortgages from the effective rate on outstanding balances. Weight resets by the original fixation schedule, and compare spending and arrears across refinancing cohorts with similar pre-war characteristics. Include lender spreads as well as the swap benchmark. A fast change in mortgage offers can coexist with slow aggregate transmission if few households actually refinance during the observation window.

questions.question: Which energy price best explains the UK inflation forecast errors?
questions.detail: Reconstruct short-horizon forecasts using the energy prices available at each meeting. Compare crude-only forecasts with ones including refined fuel, UK gas and regulated cap-setting dates. Separate the food-price miss and postponed fuel-duty change from underlying energy costs. Evaluate forecasts on later releases without using subsequent futures prices or treating a single day’s post-negotiation oil quote as the average cost paid by firms.

questions.question: Did the additional dissent change the market’s view of the reaction to future inflation news?
questions.detail: Recover pre-meeting expectations for votes, the decision and the future rate path. Compare sterling forwards immediately before and after the release with contemporaneous euro and US moves. Then check sensitivity to subsequent UK wage and inflation surprises. A change in that sensitivity could contain information about policy conditionality even when the unchanged rate itself was widely expected.
